title: The Fund XX's Gabriela Isturiz on AI, Scaling, and Empowering Women Entrepreneurs
author: Gabriela Isturiz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Isturiz shifts the focus from organisational adaptation and human control over AI to vendor-side positioning and messaging that simplify buyers’ purchasing decisions. This is practical commercial advice, but it neither endorses nor directly addresses the cluster’s central claim that AI benefits depend on workflow adaptation, training and retained human judgment.
qs: So, you make easier for the customer to buy your solution.
So it’s mastering your positioning, your messaging, and your Google Market Strategies.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Isturiz accepts selective, problem-specific deployment, qualified expert review and formal evaluation, while materially extending the cluster into professional-services economics: agentic workflow redesign can reduce operating costs and protect margins, with routine work commoditised and expert verification retaining premium value.
qs: and wedge for professional services, leveraging AI, which is how we can do more processes that are more efficient, how we can reduce our expenses, How we can optimize our workflows.
the incremental  which is still, it has to be reviewed by a qualified expert, a lawyer, an accountant.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Isturiz aligns with the cluster’s core proposition: AI will automate or streamline repetitive production work, commoditize some outputs and reduce delivery costs, while qualified professionals remain necessary for verification and may command premium rates. Her emphasis on the billable hour’s resilience reinforces the cluster’s expectation of hybrid pricing rather than wholesale displacement.

kp.k: Enterprise buyers value outcomes, not AI branding
kp.d: Isturiz argues that B2B SaaS startups should sell problem-solving value rather than AI features. She reports an unnamed product consultancy's research involving about 767 business technology users, described as mostly blue collar, comparing AI-labelled and value-focused landing pages. According to her account, generative-AI labelling lowered expectations of the product and its impact, and customers did not think they should pay more. She suggests distrust as a possible explanation, not an established finding; the transcript supplies no study citation or methodological detail beyond this account.
qs: enterprise customers do not care about your AI feature, period.
767 business tech users, mostly blue collar.
it significantly lower the expectations of the product and the potential impact.
customers are buying on the value that you provide, not on the features that you deliver

kp.k: Innovation outpaces organisational adoption and purchasing capacity
kp.d: Isturiz identifies adopting, implementing and retaining technology as a central constraint for firms and other labour-intensive professional services organisations. Existing workable solutions and proliferating narrowly targeted products make purchasing difficult. Her recommendation that founders ask whether they offer ten times the value is a positioning heuristic, not a measured adoption threshold. Separately, Gebauer observes that law firms are still struggling to articulate concrete AI benefits to clients, while Lambert describes difficulty justifying substantial technology investment to partners.
qs: are firms, organizations, able to adopt, implement, and retain these technologies at the pace that this innovation is coming at you.
I will argue that buying is harder
Am I delivering 10 times value for me to move these organizations to something, to this new frontier?
I think firms are still kind of struggling to be able to crystallize that because they’re still just kind of getting their hands around how do we use this?

kp.k: Scaling requires retention, processes and different personnel capabilities
kp.d: Drawing on her SaaS-building experience, Isturiz distinguishes problem–solution fit, product–market fit and scaling. Early customers must both pay and remain customers; she discusses five to 10 customers and being north of one or two million dollars in revenue before the next scaling frontier. Scaling then requires systematic hiring, processes and expertise in growing companies to $10 million or $20 million in revenue, rather than simply retaining the startup's original generalist approach. This is entrepreneurial guidance, not an AI-specific empirical finding.
qs: you have to have a problem solution fit
but more importantly, can you retain them?
For you to scale, you need to start incorporating processes, procedures, methods
People that have done companies taking it to $10 million in revenue, $20 million in revenue, and that changes completely the landscape.

kp.k: Incumbent distribution advantages shape startup competition and exits
kp.d: Isturiz names established legal technology vendors, including LexisNexis, Wolters Kluwer, Thomson Reuters, Roper and Litera, as competitors whose advantages include trust and existing customer distribution. She recommends narrow differentiation and faster iteration, citing eBilling Hub's focus on improving manual, spreadsheet-based incumbent offerings. Her described acquisition playbook involves winning market share and prompting customers to request integrations; she qualifies it by noting that earlier technology or team acquisitions can leave founders short of valuations achievable after stronger revenue and growth.
qs: they’re there because they have gained the trust of the market and they also had the distribution.
you really need to find one thing or a couple of things that you can do better than they do.
So when you start getting all these firms, they’re satisfied. They go and talk to the company and said, can you integrate with them?
the incumbent always, it’s kind of like on the driver’s seat because they have the distribution.

kp.k: AI erodes startups' traditional product-development speed advantage
kp.d: Isturiz argues that AI allows incumbents to create products as quickly as startups, reducing their need to wait several years for startups to develop and de-risk acquisition targets. She uses Salesforce and other enterprise software examples as cross-domain support rather than presenting measured legal-market results. Asked whether founders can still sell a product, wait out a non-compete and rebuild essentially the same offering, she says she does not believe so: AI changes the underlying workflows, making forward-looking invention more important than repetition.
qs: Right now, the incumbents are really creating amazing products, Equally as fast as startups
I don’t believe so because of the whole thing that I see with AI.
AI is also rethinking the way the old way approach to problems was done.
it’s also exposing new workflows

kp.k: Billable hours persist while routine work becomes commoditised
kp.d: Isturiz rejects a simple prediction of the billable hour's imminent disappearance, citing its resilience despite decades of forecasts and acknowledging alternative fee arrangements. She expects AI-enabled repetitive tasks to receive commodity pricing, while qualified expert review commands a premium and potentially higher hourly rates. This is her prospective account of legal and other professional services, grounded in her view that their business model sells time, rather than evidence of realised pricing changes.
qs: the billable hour has shown all of us that is incredibly resilient
What you’re selling is your time, Your time is your product
They’re going to be priced, you know, as a commodity
it has to be reviewed by a qualified expert, a lawyer, an accountant.
And we’re going to see probably increases in the billable hour for those that can do it.

kp.k: Operational efficiency offers a route to maintaining partner profits
kp.d: Isturiz argues that clients' capacity to absorb price increases is limited, making lower operating costs and improved workflows an important AI opportunity for professional services. She proposes using agents and other tools to reduce the resources required by processes and maintain margins. Although she includes people among the resources firms could reconsider, she does not quantify workforce reductions or specify changes to associate leverage or staffing structures.
qs: you can squeeze much from a client.
how you’re going to continue your profit per partners
how we can reduce our expenses
If I was using, you know, these many tools, resources, people, How can I start using agents or the like?
to really maintain my margins, right, but reducing the cost.

kp.k: Browser-using agents could automate administrative legal workflows
kp.d: Isturiz describes personally testing OpenAI Operator on website research and sees potential for agents to perform operational tasks involving multiple websites, including invoice-related and filing workflows. She presents these as emerging capabilities and possibilities, explicitly acknowledging that Operator is imperfect and had only been available for a couple of weeks. Her account is an anecdotal demonstration, not a reliability evaluation or evidence of production deployment in law firms.
qs: I was playing with operator, I gave them a list of things of websites, just go into the research.
It’s not perfect. It’s only been out for, you know, a couple of weeks or something like that.
Now we have the intelligent agents. And now we have the agents that manage the other agents.
startups really, really need to be aware of these capabilities.

kp.k: AI reopens law firms' build-versus-buy decisions
kp.d: Isturiz argues that democratised development tools give firms capabilities increasingly similar to startups, creating a competitive frontier within customer organisations themselves. She sees potential for innovative firms to build using existing tools, subject to security and privacy boundaries. Gebauer separately says internal development is already occurring and that firms now employ people capable of it who would not have been on their rosters a few years earlier. Neither speaker supplies adoption statistics.
qs: the firms have very similar capabilities that my startup has
I see a lot of potential for them leveraging existing tools within the boundaries of security, privacy and all that to build themselves.
And you’re seeing that. You’re seeing that already happening.
It’s been so democratized that you have the same capabilities that I might have in my startup

kp.k: Go-to-market execution becomes central as technology commoditises
kp.d: In her concluding forecast, Isturiz identifies positioning, messaging, customer acquisition and retention—not technology creation alone—as the decisive challenge for legal and professional services technology providers. For buyers, she recommends current frameworks, policies and procedures for evaluating proliferating products instead of relying on playbooks from three, five or 10 years earlier. Her argument concerns organisational technology selection, not legal-work evaluation or model benchmarking.
qs: the real thing that needs to be mastered is not the tech itself, it’s go to market.
the complexity to acquire and retain customers.
Do you have frameworks, policies, and even procedures of how you’re going to evaluate in the time that we are right now?
you are not relying on the playbooks that you have five years ago, 10 years ago, or even three years ago.

kp.k: Women founders need capital and network access
kp.d: Isturiz frames The Fund XX's women-focused investment mission around funding and access disparities. She reports that in 2024 VCs deployed 190 billion, with 3% of dollars going to women, 6% of deals involving women founders or all-women teams, and 15% involving mixed teams. These are her reported figures; the transcript provides no underlying dataset or precise category definitions. She argues that capital and access to networks, customers and further funding support the next generation of women builders, and defends intentional investment despite political pushback.
qs: last year in 2024, 190 billions were deployed by VCs in different stages.
Out of that 190 billion, 3 % dollar-wise went to women.
6 % of deals involved women founders or all women teams
15 % of the deals that got VC money were mixed teams.
But they need two things.  Capital and access

kp.k: Investment-manager representation also constrains women's entrepreneurial funding
kp.d: Isturiz describes the funding challenge as twofold: insufficient capital reaching women and mixed founding teams, and limited representation of women among investment decision-makers. She states that women represent less than 12% of investment managers and advocates increasing women's participation as investors in venture capital, not only funding recipients. This is a broader entrepreneurial ecosystem argument, not a demonstrated AI-specific effect.
qs: the funding challenge, it’s, it’s twofold
we only represent less than 12 % of the investment managers.
we also want to present opportunity for more women to understand this asset class as an opportunity for them to invest.
it’s not just the funding to the entrepreneurs and to the founders, but also how can we bring more women into the investment

kp.k: Fund economics favour scalable, capital-compatible early-stage technology ventures
kp.d: Isturiz says The Fund XX had made 30 investments and was preparing a second fund. Its sector-agnostic strategy targets pre-seed or seed technology and technology-enabled companies valued under $10 million, allowing meaningful ownership. Selection also depends on markets large enough to generate fund-returning outcomes, founder sales ability, energy, responsiveness and alignment with the fund. She distinguishes worthwhile community businesses from venture-return requirements and excludes capital-intensive areas she describes as FDA-approved DeepTech.
qs: have made 30 amazing investments
pre-seed or seed, developing tech companies or tech enabled companies with valuations under $10 million.
we need to have meaningful participation in this round.
these companies need to be fund returnable.
we’re looking for those outsized returns.
FDA approved DeepTech because they’re heavy capital-demanding

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Isturiz argues that enterprise buyers purchase value rather than AI features, and that emphasizing AI branding can depress product expectations without supporting a price premium.
pts.d: At 01:28, Gabriela Isturiz applies this argument to enterprise B2B SaaS, including the legal-tech startups under discussion. She characterizes AI as a force multiplier but advises founders to balance AI terminology with a clear account of the customer problem solved. Her reported research concerns business technology users rather than a specifically legal sample.

pts.k: Isturiz claims that AI makes product creation unprecedentedly easy, shifting the competitive challenge toward adoption, positioning, distribution, and customer acquisition and retention.
pts.d: At 07:23 and 48:57, she contrasts rapid innovation with firms' capacity to adopt, implement, and retain technology. She argues that as technology becomes commoditized, go-to-market execution becomes harder and more important. Her reference to delivering ten times the value is a proposed switching proposition, not a measured productivity result.

pts.k: Isturiz argues that AI weakens startups' historical speed advantage over incumbents and undermines the strategy of repeatedly building and selling essentially the same product.
pts.d: At 22:03–27:45, she explains that incumbents already possess customer trust and distribution, and now can develop AI products as quickly as startups rather than waiting years to acquire de-risked innovations. She cites Salesforce and a company rendered as 'HotSpot' in the transcript as cross-domain illustrations. Asked about rebuilding the same product after an acquisition and non-compete, she says she does not believe that model remains viable because AI changes both problem-solving approaches and workflows. She nevertheless sees substantial opportunities for genuinely new approaches.

pts.k: Isturiz predicts pricing differentiation rather than the disappearance of hourly billing: commoditized work becomes commodity-priced while qualified expert review attracts premium rates.
pts.d: At 29:37, she describes the billable hour as resilient and expects evolution under AI-driven workflow optimization. Repetitive tasks become cheaper, but qualified human review remains necessary and potentially commands higher hourly rates. This is a forecast, not evidence of an observed market-wide pricing change.

pts.k: Isturiz identifies AI-enabled operating-cost reduction and workflow automation as the main opportunity for protecting professional-services margins.
pts.d: At 29:37–34:12, she argues that clients' willingness to pay limits continued rate increases, making operational efficiency important to profit per partner. She proposes agents as possible alternatives to some existing tools, resources, and people in workflows. She identifies website-based research and invoice-related activities as potential applications, without quantifying savings or predicting specific job losses.

pts.k: Isturiz claims that democratized AI development tools make internal technology building more feasible for law firms, changing the build-versus-buy calculation.
pts.d: At 34:12–37:57, she says firms increasingly have development capabilities comparable to startups. Innovative organizations may use existing tools to build solutions themselves, subject to security and privacy constraints. This creates another source of competition for vendors. She invokes Cursor as an illustration of the value of accelerating software development, not as a measured legal-services deployment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of a reported marketing study, Isturiz's entrepreneurial experience, selected company examples, and personal experimentation rather than legal-task benchmarks.
pts.d: For AI branding, Isturiz describes an unnamed product consultancy's study of approximately 767 business technology users, mostly described as blue collar, comparing AI-led and value-led landing pages. She reports lower expectations and no perceived willingness to pay more, but supplies no effect sizes, study date, or full methodological details in the transcript. For competitive dynamics, she draws on building and selling legal-tech businesses, including eBilling Hub, and examples of incumbent agent offerings. For automation, she reports trying Operator on website research. She also reports that Cursor was predicted to reach $100 million in revenue in two years and cites fundraising figures, without identifying an underlying source. Her pricing and margin claims are reasoned forecasts; no quantified legal-market evidence is supplied for them.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Isturiz presents most developments as current or emerging at the time of the 2025 interview, with no firm deadline for market-wide change.
pts.d: She describes Operator as only weeks old and imperfect. Adoption depends on delivering enough value to justify switching, not merely on technical availability. Her five-year reference concerns founders' strategic vision rather than a dated prediction. Premium pricing is qualified by expertise and clients' ability or willingness to pay; internal building is qualified by organizational capability, security, and privacy. She urges technology buyers to update assessment frameworks rather than rely on older procurement approaches.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are legal-tech vendors and founders, incumbent software providers, law firms as technology buyers and builders, professional-services experts, and their clients.
pts.d: Startups face harder differentiation, distribution, retention, and exit strategies. Incumbents combine established distribution with faster development. Law firms must select and assess a growing supply of tools while potentially building internally and automating operations. Lawyers and other qualified experts may receive a premium for reviewing commoditized output, while partners seek margin preservation through lower costs. Clients' demand for value and limits on price increases constrain the business model. Isturiz explicitly extends the analysis beyond law to accounting, consulting, and engineering; she does not offer a quantified employment forecast or an access-to-justice claim.
